Battle of the Atlantic. The Battle of the Atlantic was a prolonged naval and aerial struggle lasting from September 1939 to May 1945 for control of the sea lanes supplying Britain, the Soviet Union, and Allied war production. German U-boats and surface raiders attacked merchant shipping and troop transports, while the Allies developed convoy tactics, anti-submarine weapons like depth charges and sonar, and long-range aircraft to counter the threat. The battle was Britain's existential crisis as starvation and resource depletion threatened if convoys failed. Allied technological innovation and industrial capacity eventually overwhelmed German submarines. Winning the Atlantic allowed the Allies to supply and reinforce Britain for the eventual invasion of Europe.

The Atlantic was the lifeline connecting Britain to North America and the rest of the world. Britain depended on transatlantic convoys for food, fuel, and war materiel. German U-boats, coordinated under Admiral Karl Dönitz, sought to starve Britain by sinking merchant shipping faster than it could be replaced. The Allies, especially Britain, lacked sufficient escorts and anti-submarine weapons early in the war. U-boat wolf packs hunted in coordinated groups.

German surface raiders including Admiral Graf Spee and Bismarck and U-boats inflicted heavy losses on Allied shipping. The loss of the battleship Prince of Wales and battlecruiser Repulse in 1941 shocked Britain. By 1942, U-boats sank over eight million tons of shipping. At this rate, Britain would be starved into surrender. American Lend-Lease aid from 1941 began replenishing British losses, but the danger remained acute as some months saw sinkings exceed new construction.

British codebreakers broke German U-boat radio codes called Enigma, allowing convoys to be rerouted around wolf packs. Improved radar and sonar detection increased U-boat losses. The Allies introduced escort carriers, long-range Liberator aircraft, and more escorts per convoy as U-boat sinkings rose sharply. By May 1943, Dönitz withdrew U-boats from the Atlantic, admitting defeat. The battle claimed thirty-five hundred Allied ships sunk and over seventy thousand merchant seamen killed, while German losses were seven hundred eighty-four U-boats and twenty-eight thousand submariners. Allied control of the Atlantic enabled the supply of Britain, the invasion of North Africa, and the buildup for D-Day.
